bp: A public company’s annual 10-K filing is meant to tell investors what the business is, what risks it faces, how management understands the year, and what may happen next. The useful signal is often not the whole report. It is the change from last year: a new warning, a softened claim, a removed discussion, or a fresh description of pressure in the market. The paper serves that reading task. It asks how to turn two long Management Discussion and Analysis sections into a measurable account of what management newly says and what it stops saying. That matters because investors already read annual changes carefully, but the reports contain repeated legal and operational language that can swamp the few sentences where the story actually moved. The method is therefore not just sentiment analysis. It is an attempt to measure narrative change before measuring tone, so financial text becomes evidence about shifting disclosure rather than a pile of repeated words.
wh: The hard part is that 10-K language is both meaningful and repetitive. A sentence can be copied from one year to the next because the legal risk remains, because lawyers prefer stable wording, or because the company is preserving a standard description. If a system scores the full document, those repeated passages keep voting every year even when they carry no new information about the current change. At the same time, the important change may be small: one added sentence about demand weakness, one deleted paragraph about growth plans, or a rewritten risk description. Simple word counts struggle because they treat every occurrence as current evidence. Ordinary sentiment scoring also struggles because a long filing can sound negative every year due to required risk language. The central tension is separating disclosure motion from disclosure background. The paper must decide which sentences are kept, deleted, and added before it can ask whether the company’s true narrative tone moved.
naive: A smart beginner would take the current year’s 10-K, run a financial sentiment tool over all words or sentences, and compare that score with last year’s score. That seems reasonable because a gloomier document should produce a more negative score. The failure is that the document is not newly written from scratch. Large amounts of boilerplate are repeated, so unchanged risk language can dominate both years. Another beginner move would be to compare word counts directly, but small wording edits, sentence reordering, and repeated phrases can make that noisy. The thing investors care about is not whether the report contains negative words in general. It is whether newly introduced language is more or less positive than the language removed from the prior report.
ap: The core idea is to change the unit of analysis from whole-document tone to edit-level tone. The paper first lines up two consecutive filings, year t and year t+1, at the sentence level. Each sentence is treated as a disclosure object whose status can be kept, removed, or newly introduced. To decide that status, the method compares the meaning of sentences rather than relying only on exact matching, so a sentence can be recognized as essentially repeated even when surface wording changes. After that separation, the method ignores the kept material when measuring new narrative direction. It scores the financial tone of the added sentences and the deleted sentences, then subtracts the deleted average from the added average. The resulting Core Sentiment signal asks a focused question: did the company add language that sounds more positive or negative than what it removed?
mech: The mechanism starts with a cleaned and standardized pair of 10-K filings for the same company in consecutive years. The relevant input section is Management Discussion and Analysis, because that is where management describes operations, strategy, conditions, and outlook in narrative form. First, the text is broken into sentences for year t and year t+1. Second, each sentence is turned into a compact meaning-based representation: a list of numbers that places similar sentences near one another for comparison. This is what the abstract calls sentence embeddings; the important point is that sentences are converted into comparable coordinates so the system can judge whether two sentences say nearly the same thing even without identical words. Third, the method compares sentences across the two years. If a sentence in the newer filing closely matches one in the older filing, it is labeled Kept and treated as repeated background. If an older sentence has no matching successor, it is labeled Deleted. If a newer sentence has no matching predecessor, it is labeled Added. Fourth, the Added and Deleted groups are passed through FinBERT-tone, a sentiment model tuned for financial language. Fifth, the average tone of Added content is compared with the average tone of Deleted content. The output is a net change signal, Core Sentiment, plus an edit-level decomposition of what stayed, disappeared, and appeared.
math: The main mathematical idea is comparison under compression. A sentence is too rich to compare by hand at scale, so the method compresses each sentence into a numeric description that tries to keep the parts of meaning useful for matching. Closeness then becomes measurable: if two sentence descriptions are near one another, the system treats them as likely repetitions or near-repetitions; if they are far apart, it treats one as removed or newly introduced. This is a similarity problem, where the hard choice is deciding which differences matter. A legal phrase with small wording changes should probably count as kept, while a new risk disclosure should not be swallowed as a harmless rewrite. The second idea is differencing. Instead of using the absolute sentiment level of the new filing, the method measures added tone minus deleted tone. A difference is useful when the stable background is large, because subtracting removed language from added language asks what changed rather than what exists. The third idea is averaging noisy judgments. FinBERT-tone assigns sentiment to individual financial sentences, and averaging over Added and Deleted groups reduces the influence of one odd sentence. The tradeoff is detail versus reliability: compression and averaging make a scalable signal, but they can hide subtle rhetorical shifts or depend too much on sentence matching quality.
dots: This paper sits in the conference’s financial text analysis theme, but it also connects to broader text mining and information retrieval ideas in the repo. Like retrieval papers, it depends on meaningful sentence comparison: the system must find which old and new sentences belong together before it can decide what is new. Like sequence and temporal papers, it treats order across time as evidence; the same company’s report at year t is not an unrelated document but the baseline for year t+1. Like information-focused papers, it asks which text actually changes the reader’s uncertainty. Kept boilerplate carries little new information, while added and deleted passages rule out one old narrative and introduce another. It also neighbors sentiment and finance work, but with a sharper object than ordinary tone classification. The paper’s contribution is to make sentiment conditional on edits, turning a noisy document-level label into a change-level signal.
ww: The method should work better than a full-document word or sentiment count because it matches the way an informed human reads these filings. An investor does not give equal attention to every repeated risk sentence each year. They look for what management added, removed, or rephrased because those edits reveal what the company now wants, needs, or is required to disclose. By labeling kept text first, the system removes the largest source of false weight: boilerplate that remains negative or positive but unchanged. By comparing Added against Deleted content, it also handles the fact that narrative change has two sides. A company may add cautious language while deleting confident language, and the combination matters more than either side alone. Meaning-based sentence matching helps because 10-K language can be lightly edited without becoming substantively new. Financially tuned sentiment helps because words that sound neutral in everyday language may carry a specific tone in filings. Together, these pieces align the measurement with the practical question: what changed in the company’s story, and in what tonal direction?
po: The payoff is a reproducible signal for annual disclosure change. The abstract says the method uses cleaned and standardized 10-K corpora, including EDGAR-CORPUS, together with the Flex10K preprocessing pipeline, so other analysts can rebuild the comparison rather than rely on private document cleaning. It also reports that Core Sentiment outperforms conventional bag-of-words sentiment measures. In practical terms, the method gives investors and researchers a cleaner way to quantify whether management’s narrative became more optimistic or pessimistic after removing repeated background text from the measurement.
limits: The claims depend on several assumptions. Sentence matching must correctly separate true boilerplate from meaningful rewrites; if the comparison is too loose, new disclosures may be mislabeled as kept, and if it is too strict, minor wording changes may look like real edits. FinBERT-tone must also read financial sentence tone reliably in MD&A language. The abstract reports outperformance over bag-of-words sentiment, but it does not specify here which prediction target, time period, or evaluation design proves economic usefulness. The method measures disclosed narrative change, not the full condition of the company or management’s private beliefs.
